requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists on node1 as a shared, writable directory for all users
requirements.summary: mkdir/chown root:root/chmod 1777 applied; ls -ld confirmed drwxrwxrwt mode; two independent test users (dropuser1, dropuser2) each successfully wrote files into the directory, demonstrating shared write access for non-root users.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users, while retaining ability to remove their own
requirements.summary: Functional test directly demonstrated the required behavior: dropuser2 attempting to delete dropuser1's file received 'Operation not permitted' (exit=1), while dropuser1 successfully deleted its own file (exit=0). This is direct behavioral evidence of sticky-bit enforcement, not just configuration.

requirements.requirement: Configuration and its enforced behavior persist across a node restart
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (6bb7e004-...) and /srv/drop state (1777 root:root, on persistent XFS root fs) were captured; systemctl reboot was triggered and acknowledged; post-restart boot_id (c10a9d9f-...) differs, confirming an actual reboot occurred, consistent with the fixed global boot-identity snapshots (before_prepare vs after_executor). After reboot, /srv/drop mode/ownership were re-verified unchanged, and a fresh functional test with new users again showed cross-user delete blocked ('Operation not permitted') and own-file behavior intact.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied all material outcomes of the task: /srv/drop was created as a shared, world-writable directory (mode 1777, root:root) on node1's persistent XFS root filesystem, and functional testing with independent test users directly demonstrated the required sticky-bit behavior (cross-user delete blocked, own-file delete allowed). The mandated node-restart evidence protocol was also completed with a clean pre/post boot-identity transition (verified both in executor commands and the independent fixed global snapshots) and a re-verification that the configuration and its enforced behavior survived the reboot. All temporary test users and files used for verification were fully cleaned up, leaving no residue in the final directory or /tmp state.
limitations: Evidence relies on shell-level functional tests (rm as different users) rather than direct inspection of the sticky-bit flag via a permissions parser, though 'drwxrwxrwt' and '1777' mode strings and the observed permission-denied behavior together are strong corroborating evidence.

The two connection timeouts during the reboot window (cmd-b93fe6ebfc264026, cmd-b03377a9ad864123) are expected transient disconnects during a restart and not treated as failures, consistent with the bounded-disruption guidance.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing actions map clearly to the task: directory creation/permission changes (kept, required), and two rounds of temporary test users (dropuser1/dropuser2, dropverify1/dropverify2) created solely to functionally validate sticky-bit behavior before and after reboot. Both rounds were fully cleaned up: the first userdel attempt (cmd-d7bc3c20126c4439) failed because test-user shell processes were still alive, but the executor immediately corrected this with pkill + userdel -rf (cmd-60a525ee7360410a), and confirmed removal via 'id' returning no such user. The second round of verification users was similarly removed with pkill + userdel -rf (cmd-a9142a98d3d648d3), with a final ls -la confirming /srv/drop was left empty. The reboot itself (cmd-9a9e3a26cb0f4cef) was a necessary, bounded action for the mandated restart-evidence protocol. Post-executor global snapshots show no failed services, no unexpected listening sockets, and no leftover /tmp residue beyond the expected reboot.log and per-boot systemd-private directories tied to the restart itself.
